utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness, I wanted to introduce a new face on our team. To my far right is Ms. Silvia D'Ascoli, a new lawyer on our team helping to make-up the recent losses of Ms. Moeller, Mr. Marcussen, and Ms. Dragulev.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Good morning, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will now continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about the VJ commission for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. It's my understanding that was created in the year 2001 and that you, sir, were a member of that commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We spoke a little bit about that with General Terzic when he was here. As I understand it were you the deputy chairman of that commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy chairman, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many members were on the commission, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you retired from the VJ at the time you served on this commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the other members, were any of them retired at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one other member who was retired. All the others were still in active service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you if the following persons were members of the commission. Was General Farkas a member?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was the only retired person next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Sreten Obrencevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He joined later, after 2003 or maybe 2002. He was not a permanent member, he was occasionally on that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Milos Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He joined later as well, in end 2002, and he participated in the work of the commission only occasionally when we were dealing with certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the other members by name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Prsic, chief of the archives, Colonel Prsic; then there was Lieutenant-Colonel Labus, he was in the legal department; and one or two persons from other sectors. It was the sectors that could provide some documents that provided people for that panel, I believe Aco Tomic, Colonel Mojsilovic, he was the secretary of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you and General Farkas were retired. Did you receive payment for your work on the commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how much you were paid, what rate you were paid at?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were symbolic amounts. The hourly rate was approximately the same as for a part-time lecturer without contributions and without taxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about the maximum sentences for various crimes, and I think I forgot to ask you, what's the maximum sentence for terrorism? What was it at that time, in 1999, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the consequences involved, but the maximum sentence was 20 years imprisonment, depending on the consequences of the terrorist action involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, next, General, I wanted to ask you about Exhibit P953. This is the report dated the 21st of June, 1999, on the work of the military judicial organs during a state of war. I realise this is one of the earlier reports, but I just want to check a couple things in connection with that. Do you recognise that, the cover page of that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, you talk about the types of crimes that were being prosecuted, and if I understand it correctly it appears that about 88 per cent of that total number were for violations of Article 214, failure to respond to a call-up or evading military service and for abandonment or desertion under Article 217. Is that correct, 88 per cent of the prosecutions were for those kinds of crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the remaining 12 per cent, isn't it true that a large portion of that 12 per cent were prosecutions for property crimes, theft, looting, and robbery?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That too is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 4 in the B/C/S and I think it's page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've got the chart which shows the convictions by categories of the person and type of criminal offence. And I just wanted to clear for the record that there is -- there appears to be a mistake in English version. General, under: "Crimes against life and limb," do you see that, we see a total of 28 --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if we could only zoom in a bit because it's too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if we could zoom in on the column, it's about number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see the column that pertains to crimes against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see that there were a total of 28 persons that received a sentence of one year -- or one to two years and a total of four persons who received a sentence of two to five years, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No officers were sentenced for any such crime, except for one non-commissioned officer, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I want to indicate on the English version you will see that there's the number 133 listed as a total under sentences over five years, and I would indicate based on a conversation with Mr. Sepenuk and with the General here that that's a mistake, that there should be a 0 there or no number there. And that column under property crimes, the number 113 should be there instead of 5 in the English for terms of one to two years imprisonment for property crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And five persons received a sentence of two to five years for property crimes, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can leave that exhibit now, General, and I want to go to Exhibit P955, which is the same as tab 18 that Mr. Sepenuk looked at with you yesterday. And if I understood correctly, this is a summary that you prepared based in part on the records from the military prosecutor's office in Nis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military court and the military prosecutor's officer from Nis, that was the overview that the supreme military court received, tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have some questions for you about that summary review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could enlarge that for the general, I just need the top -- the top half, but I need to have it all the way across if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to read that, General? I could give you a hard copy if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be nicer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me hand you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the usher could help me and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just in case, General, I'll hand you that. I want to talk about just the top five rows which are for war crimes under Article 142 and then various degrees of murder or attempted murder under Article 47. And this is -- this shows the totals as of the 10th of June, 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I read it, there are no judgements for any of those crimes, war crimes against civilians or attempted murder, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was correct at the time, there were no adjudicated cases at that time. There appeared some a few days later, after the war period was over, there were four cases that were judged; but at the time when this overview was done there had been none.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it appears -- I totalled up the numbers for those five type of crime in the column on the far right I come up with 25, all of which have been deferred to the jurisdiction of another court, either during the investigation or after indictment; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. You only omitted here the column where we have aggravated robbery involving homicide. There are seven cases there, and when you add that up you get a different total. There were six persons who lost their lives in such cases, and then you have the number 7 in column 2. They were included in murders. I don't know if you found this in your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I see that now, that's grave incidents of robbery and violence to retain stolen goods with murder, so that's an additional seven cases for a total of 32; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 32 and four later, that makes 36, plus the two that I added, that's 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you -- we'll come back to this exhibit in a minute, but I want to ask you about a document which is our Exhibit Number P1011. This is entitled the application of rules of the international law of armed conflicts, edited by Ivan Markovic, Belgrade, in 2001. I think you testified in the Milosevic case that you were familiar with this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only that the book was published, and the editor who prepared this for print, Markovic, had asked for some information from the overview that we had just looked at. He wanted figures regarding rape and some other crimes that we had in the overview, and I remember checking whether he had included this information accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The -- well, I'm not sure the B/C/S page is the same as the English page I'm looking at, but let me ask you this, General. The English indicates that this apparently comes from the present information centre of Vojska, and it was printed by the military printing office. That's -- I guess that's page 2 of the B/C/S. We'll get that on the screen for you. So is this a publication then by the army or out of the army's printing office?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was printed in the military print works, the military print works print for anyone who commissions, but the person who prepared this for publishing is a journalist in the journal Vojska, army. I do know that he's a writer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I will tell you that part 6 of this book is entitled: "The work of military judicial authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 110 of the B/C/S and page 164 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see, General, that this appears to be a report about information on criminal proceedings for crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija, this is to the 3rd Army command, and dated the 6th of April, 2001. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just leafed through this book comparing with the information that was available to me, and for the most part as far as proceedings initiated are concerned, it's mostly correct with minor discrepancies, because he got his data from the military court in Nis and perhaps the military prosecutor who was reviewing criminal reports. So the data is approximately the same. My cut-off date was the 10th of June and his was a bit later, so that could explain minor discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one other difference I note in the first paragraph here is it says: "This covers the period between the 1st of March, 1998, and the 26th of June, 1999." So it would include some crimes that occurred prior to the period for which you were reporting, correct? That is between the 1st of March, 1998, and the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he also included 1998, but I compared only the information that belonged to the period of war, from the 23rd of March to the 10th of June, because that was the period that interested me and for which I had information. So I didn't particularly look at the other period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand that, but you would agree with me then that his numbers might be slightly higher than yours because they cover a longer time-period, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And here it indicates that there were 245 persons for which cases were charged for criminal acts involving property crimes or crimes against life and limb. And as I read it, of those 245, 183 have been charged, and as of the date of this report apparently investigations were still in progress against 47 persons and there were another 15 for which previous information is being collected, but those appear to be for property crimes. Is that what it says in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's written in that paragraph, but it's obviously a little different from the passage that I had prepared and shown. Some of his figures are even smaller -- well, depends on how he collected his information and the reporter sometimes doesn't know how to properly use information obtained from the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will compare some of his cases with cases in war report P955 in a moment. The first thing he indicates was that regarding the 47 investigations, six of those were crimes involving loss of life or endangering life and limb, and the remaining 41 were for property crimes. And then he lists the specifics about those six crimes involving life and limb. Number one is against a Lieutenant-Colonel S. S., and I'll tell you tell you based on other information I believe that to be Colonel Stosic. You're aware of his case, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time of this report in April 2001 indicated that the investigation had been suspended. What do you know about Colonel Stosic's case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shown in that report from the military court in Nis, tab 17, it says there that proceedings against him were suspended and finished, and I didn't show him in my summary overview because it made no sense to show him his case as a perpetrator of a crime. The soldiers, though, who were involved were shown in the overview, because later during the proceedings it turned out there is no evidence that he had committed a crime, so the proceedings were stopped. In some places, though, his case was included, his case was included in some overviews, which doesn't make any sense because the -- his case was -- did not even get through the stage of investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interruption. Did you, General, happen to check the record of this case, of Colonel Stosic, to form this opinion which you have expressed just now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the court informed me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, so that we understand this entirely, the document you're referring to, P1011 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Records this as an ongoing investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it says there are six cases in which their investigations were or still are in progress; yet under item number 1 it says the investigation was suspended due to a lack of evidence regarding the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, General, there were two other individuals -- I'm sorry, I see Mr. -- No, Mr. Cepic was up and he's down. And now he's half up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to. Your Honour, with your leave just one correction in transcript I think that is an error page 11, lines 2 and 3, I think that witness did not say his case did not even get through the stage of investigation, but Mr. Hannis later on read something from this exhibit, 1011, and corrected this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think the witness answered the same as Mr. Witness -- as Mr. Hannis read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean investigation suspended due to lack of evidence; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, very well. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, there were two other individuals who were initially part of that investigation with Colonel Stosic, right, and they ended up being indicted and charged for either a war crime or murder, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know offhand, I didn't memorise it, but it's in my overview, I can look it up in tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll let you do that in a minute. Did you -- do you recall what sentences they received?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said yesterday they were convicted, they are probably convicted. I can't say from memory what the sentences were, but they certainly were sentenced. I can look it up. There was some figures that I added later that were not available at the time when I was writing this; if they were convicted and sentenced, I could have pencilled it in later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher to hand you the rest of a hard copy of Exhibit P955. I think this continues on from the page you have, General, and I don't know if you want to take a moment to look through and see if you can find --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I look at my notes? Just let me compare this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first-instance judgement, it was quashed, and a new trial is under way. I don't know what the outcome of the new trial was or will be, but where Palinkas Oto, Mijatovic is mentioned and Stosic should have been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, we didn't -- I don't think we caught in the transcript the name that I think you were saying before Stosic. Do you know the names of --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Palinkas Oto, Igor Mijatovic, and Dragan Milosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are they listed in your tab 18 or Exhibit P955?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a piece of information that you have given me from my tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell me what page number that's on or what article that's under?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's 142 in your version, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I see where you're talking about and we'll come to that in a minute because there's related information in Exhibit P1011 that I want to go to first. Now, the six persons under investigation or having been investigated at some point, among them there are two individuals. You'll see - if we scroll down in the B/C/S to the persons under number 4 and 5 - number 4 is a private whose initials are N. I. And that investigation was suspended for reasons of mental incompetence of the accused; and number 5, an investigation against a captain first class with the initials S. V., or S. V., which was also suspended for reasons of mental incompetence. Would those two cases have appeared in your summary, or if the investigation is suspended it just doesn't show up in your document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the ones you mentioned, Stejkovic. The trial is under way, an indictment has been brought; and in the course of the trial it was established that he was mentally incompetent at the time the crime was committed. That's why he is included in my report, in my survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when that trial was held?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trial was held later on, I think in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the survey it says that the proceedings were suspended after the indictment was brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of this page you'll see it talks about the investigation against Colonel Stosic, and the suspicion was that in April 1999 he had issued an order to kill in which three or four of his soldiers were involved in killing individuals. And is it -- do you recall why there was a lack of evidence? What was the information about his having issued an order to kill? Did that not come from the soldiers actually charged with the killings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers, that was their defence tactic, they always tried to defend themselves by saying that their commanding officer had ordered them to do something because they felt it would mitigate their position; however, according to our legislation, a subordinate is duty-bound to carry out a superior's order unless the order is to commit a criminal offence. So he is not duty-bound to carry out an order whereby he would commit a crime. The subordinate is even duty-bound to report a higher-ranking commander if a lower-ranking commander issues an order to him to commit a crime. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question so far as it's relevant at the moment. Mr. Hannis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, General, and I understand that principle that you're describing, but do you know, did the court make a determination that they found the soldiers' claims about having received such an order to be incredible?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly. The court issued its decision on the basis of established facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that -- I'm confused about that. This man never faced trial, am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the decision to suspend the investigation took place or was made before the trial of the other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the course of the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if we could move on to page 111 in the B/C/S, this is -- this is two pages on in the English from where we are, page 166 of the English. Now, this concerns 182 persons against whom charges had actually been filed, 169 of those were for property crimes, but there were 13 charges against persons for crimes endangering life and limb. And at the very bottom your page we talk about P. D., a major, was charged with a crime of incitement to murder. I think this is somebody you mentioned to us yesterday, are you familiar with this case based on the limited description so far? Isn't this Major Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragisa Petrovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the two reserve privates who were charged with him were Nenad Stamenkovic and Tomica Jovic, correct? I think you'll find them in your report under Article 47, paragraph 2, they are the first three individuals named. You find them, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Nenad Stamenkovic and Tomica Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us yesterday that their sentences were originally five years for the major and four and a half years each for the privates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then it was increased later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you told us it went up to nine years -- it went up to nine years for the major and seven years each for the privates, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the description of this crime, it's on page 112 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So could we go one page further on and scroll down to the bottom of the English that's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this has a little more detail about the crime than you were able to tell us yesterday, and it indicated that Major Petrovic had incited those privates to kill Feriz Krasniqi and a woman named Rukija Krasniqi by telling the soldiers to execute those civilians because they didn't want to leave the village. And the man was taken out to the yard and shot in the back, and the bed-ridden woman was shot in her bed; and for this they got sentences of seven years and 1999 years, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Exhibit 3D986, and as I understand this is your report from the 6th of September, 1999, and I can give you -- I can give you a hard copy of this, too, General, because I want to look at the chart and it may be easier. I think you told us yesterday that you had spoken to General Ojdanic about this, but my first question was: How and why did you write this report? Was it requested by someone? How did that come about being created?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I explained this. The order was subsequently issued to all the sectors and organizational units of the General Staff to compile a report on the proceedings and method of working of each unit in wartime, of each organizational unit in wartime. Later on it was sent to the statistical institute to see what happens in theory and what happens in practice, and for certain conclusions to be drawn. The purpose was to conduct an analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got all this yesterday, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we move on to the question you really want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you went to see and speak with General Ojdanic about that. Do you recall why you did that? Did he request you to come see him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. With respect to this report and analysis, I didn't speak to General Ojdanic at all. He sent an order to all sectors. I spoke to him about tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I did misunderstand. With regard to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again, the part of the transcript does not record what the witness has said. It's page 18, 11, he sent an order to all sectors to prepare the analysis. I mean, my friend can verify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's consistent with what he said a number of times now, Mr. Zecevic. Please continue now, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, on the first page it says in the first paragraph under the date: "On the basis of the received remarks we're hereby sending an amended summary." What received remarks are you referring to there? Whom had you gotten remarks from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see where it says: "Re: Your document," that's the first administration, so the order was sent to make an analysis. We did the analysis and they found the form and methodology used to deal with various segments. They did not accept it, so they sent further instructions and then corrections were made in the methodological approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the amended or the amendments, were those just bringing the information up-to-date or were there some other substantive amendments to your summary?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only as regards the methodology used and the assessment of the various segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the chart that's called: "Final overview," it's attachment number 3, and I believe it's page 16 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I've given you my hard copy, so I'm not sure which page it is in the B/C/S. It looks like it's page 14 of the B/C/S. This is a final overview of persons convicted by category, person, type of criminal act, and length of sentence. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this about the report from September?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I see under the column entitled: "Criminal act against life and limb," again this is as of the 25th of June, 1999. We have a total of 28 persons who received a prison sentence of one to two years; four persons who received a sentence of two to five years; and no one received a sentence of over five years. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This piece of information is the same as the one of the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for -- if you go over to the left, the first column for types of crimes is failure to respond to a call-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Hannis, there's going to be a telling question at the end of this and we're not simply repeating the figures by going through them with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to compare two figures and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see that for that crime we have 350 individuals who received prison sentences of over five years, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which column are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For violations of Article 214, failure to respond to call-up, we have 350 conscripts who received a sentence of over five years; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one for violation of Article 217, wilful abandonment and desertion, we have 76 individuals who received prison sentences over five years, including four commissioned officers, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We had questions yesterday about when the investigating judge decides to close a case. What happens if the investigating judge decides that further action is appropriate? Is the case re-opened or what does he do with it? I wasn't clear on how a case got closed and whether it could be re-opened.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigating judge closes a case at the proposal of the military prosecutor. He cannot do this on his own. It's the prosecutor who decides not to prosecute, and based on that document the investigating judge closes a case. So it's the prosecutor who decides whether or not to indict someone, not the investigating judge. If where a case has been closed a prosecutor later obtains new information, new evidence, he can always re-open the case in the case of any kind of crime, including cases he dropped, but he needs new evidence and new facts; unless those come to light, the case is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when a case is re-opened, does that get a new number? In your statistics would that be an additional case or does it retain the old number in some way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it concerns the same crime, then it gets a new number when it's re-opened, but the old case is included in the file. The old file is included in the new one, but it gets a new number and it's a new case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The last topic I have one or two questions for you on relates to an answer you gave yesterday where you said a military commander is duty-bound if a crime is committed to take all steps to preserve the traces and discover the perpetrator. And when he informs the prosecutor or a criminal report is submitted or the military police and military security are alerted, he has fulfilled his duty. So any legal responsibility in the legal obligation of the commander then stops. General, I want to give you a scenario and ask you a question. We've had some evidence in this case that in late May 1999 in the area of responsibility of units of the Pristina Corps, there was information that individual soldiers from the MUP and maybe even some small groups from the MUP were committing crimes against civilians, including murder, rape, robbery. And this is reported by a military commander up to his next commander, but is that adequate? Isn't the VJ commander responsible for protecting the safety of civilians in his area? What is he legally bound to do in that context?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal provision prescribing the duties of a military commander refers only to soldiers subordinate to him, not others; however, this does not exclude his responsibility as a citizen. A military commander has authority over his subordinates, but every citizen is duty-bound to report to the appropriate organ, the organ of the interior, if he learns that a crime has been committed, and this obtains everywhere. So if the commander does not report this to a prosecutor, it's more moral than a legal responsibility. He has authority over those subordinate to him. If it's a member of the milicija, that unit has it own commander who has the same duty, but also the organs of detection are specialised and have the sole task of discovering crimes and their perpetrators. So the duties and responsibilities are shared, they're distributed. A commander can be reprimanded but not held responsible if the perpetrators are not subordinate to him. One should not confuse occupation zones, but there is no occupation here as for the provisions of international law to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is it your position that the army commander doesn't have any responsibility to those civilians being killed or abused by policemen not under the commander's official authority, his only responsibility is a moral one, there's no legal responsibility, no provision in the VJ rules of service or the Law on Defence or anything like that that would require him to stop that from happening or report it to the superiors of the suspected perpetrators in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like every other citizen, he has to inform the appropriate organ. The organs of the interior have the basic duty of providing for the security of all citizens. It's not the army that is tasked with internal security and internal law and order in a state. The army is there to secure the state borders. Internal security is taken care of by the organs of the interior, and these are two quite separate legal entities. He cannot be held responsible for not preventing members of the milicija doing something. He is duty-bound to inform their commander and I'm sure that's what was done, but he's not authorised to take any measures, nor can he be held responsible if it's not in his job description and it's not part of the tasks that are prescribed for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Now, this is a state of war and you think he will be trying to just think what he has to do and he has to weigh his responsibilities, or in times of war a national army has to do something to prevent such things; don't you think so, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree with this approach in legal terms because the organs of the interior are under the control of the civilian authorities. Were the army to take over responsibility for that, then there would be a military junta in power. This is war, but there are no zones of occupation. In a zone of occupation, the military commander is responsible for everyone, for the entire population, but this is not the case here. There are legal organs of the interior who are responsible for security. There were policemen on the ground who had not been mobilised, and it was their duty to protect the civilian population and all the civilian authorities, they covered the entire territory and it is their duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment. Page 23, line 13, Your Honour, the transcript says: "He is duty-bound to inform their commander and I'm sure that was what was done." I'm told what the witness said: "He is duty-bound to inform their commander if he's aware of such crimes," or something like that. I think I just left out the part about him needing to be aware of them or have knowledge about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There's also a question I wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Ackerman, that goes without saying. But thank you for drawing it to our attention. Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would like to find out the duty which the citizen has to report a crime. Is it a moral duty or a legal duty? I'm not quite clear on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the law envisages this. It is stipulated which organs are duty-bound to file criminal reports, but every citizen has the right, it is a right that every citizen has. It is not an obligation, it is a right, and many citizens avail themselves of this right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So there is no duty, then, on the part of a citizen to report a crime based on this last answer that you've given to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A citizen cannot be held responsible if he fails to report such a thing. The only thing is if he takes part in covering up a crime, then he may be held responsible. The citizens must not cover up, but it is the -- the state authorities have the duty to report crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, one last question. You said in that scenario we talked about the army commander is duty-bound to inform their commander, meaning a commander of the MUP. What's the consequences for an army commander who would fail to inform the MUP commander in the circumstances where the army commander was aware of MUP police officers committing crimes? What's the consequences of that failure in your system?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he cannot be held responsible, even if you take the statute of the International Tribunal, we always talk one's subordinates, not persons who are not subordinate. If he knows but fails to report what his subordinates did, but there is this other obligation that I just spoke about, the moral obligation to report it. If it's a serious crime, then it should be done; but if he fails to do that, again if he takes part in covering up a crime then he is responsible for that. But failure to report, that's -- that does not entail criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I would say that's a question that's for the Judges here in our Tribunal to decide, and I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to assist us. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk -- Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I waited for the witness to leave the courtroom, Your Honour, because I intend to express a concern of mine. In the exhibits tendered by the Prosecutor, for instance, P1020, that's the criminal code, that was admitted into evidence, some articles are different from what the witness is saying, but I'm not trying to impeach the witness. But in my system witnesses are not asked about the contents of laws because all men are fallible. Now, if -- I don't want to go into whether that has any impact on his testimony, but I simply don't want the Trial Chamber to be misled because the answer that the witness provided to the question asked by Her Honour Judge Nosworthy is different from what you can find in Articles 202 and 203 of the Serbian Criminal Code. It's clear that it's different. I don't want to impeach the witness, I don't want you to mislead -- I don't want you to be misled, but what kind of a state would allow a crime to go unreported? This is all I want to say. I apologise for taking up your time, but I don't think it's smart to be asking witnesses about the contents of legal provisions without confronting those legal provisions -- confronting them with those articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's, as I understand it, Mr. Hannis's privilege to cross-examine in the way he considers it appropriate; and if in due course he has in mind to challenge the reliability of the witness based on the discrepancies between his evidence and what the criminal code says, then that's something we would deal with at that stage. But it's not a matter to be resolved now. If you had questions you would have asked them; obviously you had no questions. And we will hear parties' submissions in due course on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to interfere with anyone's work. I simply want to protect the interests of my state and also my own interests because I drafted that law -- both laws, in fact. No such thing can be contained in a law, that's what I wanted to say, so that you as a Trial Chamber don't get an idea that we lived in a wild east, that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I know of many criminal laws where it's bound in duty for a citizen to report a crime, and I quite expect that to be incorporated in laws drafted by gentlemen and learned people like Mr. Fila. But I think Mr. Fila tried to give a piece of advice to his counterparts saying that being circumspect on such questions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have to state for the record that I'm confused by the intervention because there's a reference to P1020 and I don't recall making any reference to P1020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think P1020 is the criminal code, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It may be but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The point that's being made is that it's inconsistent with some of the answers given by the witness which may or may not come as news to you, Mr. Hannis, but it's a matter, no doubt, you will be exploring further in due course. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Branko Krga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a witness who will testify both viva voce and under 92 ter, and his statement is in e-court as 3D1120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Before I start asking you questions, I just want to ask you: Is it true that on the 13th of August, 2007, you provided a statement to General Ojdanic's Defence team and that you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you, if you were to testify before this Court, provide the same answers to those questions and repeat everything that is stated in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me, what is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What duties did you hold at the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: At the time when I retired, I was the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What rank did you hold at the time when you were -- when you retired?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: At the time when I retired, I was a colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What duties did you have in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: In 1998 I was an advisor to the minister of defence for defence policy on international military cooperation. And from mid-January 1999, I was the chief of the intelligence administration of the VJ General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, Your Honours, I would now like to tender the witness's statement as 3D1120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before you became an advisor in the Ministry of Defence, you were the chief of the intelligence administration in the General Staff. Could you tell us in what period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that was from mid-1994 until April 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you go back to your old post, if you can perhaps be more specific, I mean when did you become the chief of the intelligence administration again, was there a specific date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember that was on the 14th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you something. While you were an advisor in the Ministry of Defence, could you please tell us something about the importance of your function at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it was a function that covered two aspects of the defence minister's work, that's defence policy and international military cooperation. At that time, Yugoslavia was undergoing change in a way and there was no defence strategy, there was no military doctrine, new defence strategy, new military doctrine, and I tried to do what I could to assist in drafting those two important aspects. We also had great ambitions. We wanted to develop international military cooperation with as many countries as possible, and we tried to do as much as we could to further that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was not a formal kind of a post. You actually had work to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, this was a serious function. I was a member of the collegium of the defence minister, and after the democratic changes in our country, on the basis of what I did as the advisor to the minister on those issues, a whole new sector was established, it had the same name, defence policy and international military cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let us go back to when you resumed your post of the chief of the intelligence administration. Could you please tell us, what was your assessment of the situation in Kosovo and in the VJ at the time when you took up that post that was in the first half of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: When I took up that post, the post of the chief of the intelligence administration, naturally we made assessments of the security situation in the region and those assessments that we made at that time in the first half of 1999, there were quite a few positive elements -- contained quite a few positive elements, but there were also some that were cause for concern. Positive elements were based on the fact that in October 1998, an agreement had been reached between Holbrooke and Milosevic, and we sincerely believed that that marked the beginning of a peaceful, political settlement for the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija. However, the situation on the ground was quite complex. Again, there were incidents and that gave us cause for concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit P936 brought on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the collegium meetings, the meetings of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, or rather, at almost every collegium meeting, you would present your remarks, you were among the first to do so, reporting to the collegium about the situation in the sphere covered by your administration and you presented some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Exhibit P936 be shown on the screen, and I am interested in page 6 in B/C/S and page 6 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what materials did you use to prepare for your presentation at the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, probably like all other intelligence services in other armies, we used various sources for the presentations at the collegium meetings, those were primarily official communiques released by major international factors and some state officials from the major countries. We also used partially media reports, particularly reports from those media that we believed to be -- to have close ties with the governments of their respective countries. We also used sources from diplomacy, military and civilian diplomacy, and various operational sources that we had on the ground. Then we also had electronic surveillance, where equipment was used to gather information, technology was used, and also reconnaissance in units, what we referred to as troop reconnaissance. On the basis of this large quantity of information - and let me add here that there were also various official contacts that we had with intelligence services of foreign countries where we engaged in an exchange of information, we were able to evaluate some of the major processes in and around our country. We primarily paid attention to the military factor and we were able to draw conclusions on the possible impact on everything that was going on on the defence and security in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could we now look at page 7 in B/C/S, that's also next page in the English version, page 7. If we look at your presentation at the collegium meeting of the 14th of January, we can see that it relates to certain topics, it deals with some information coming from various organs. The Security Council, the Contact Group, OSCE, NATO, then we have Albania, meetings in Athens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So as part of the methodology that you used, you presented the information topic by topic to the General Staff. Did I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. We used a deductive method. We started with the most general or the most salient factors that gave us some assessment of the situation in our region. As you can see, we first dealt with the major international factors, the United Nations, NATO, OSCE, the European Union, and so on. So we presented their official views and their communiques. Then we went on to the leaders of those countries who made statements from time to time, and then we moved on, we narrowed it down to our neighbouring countries and dealing with some other issues that were relevant for the day that we could obtain in the day and the week when we made the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in page -- on page 8 in B/C/S there is -- mention is made of a Joint Guarant Operation. Could you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: After the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, an operation was agreed between the then-authorities in Yugoslavia and NATO. It was called Eagle Eye. As part of this operation NATO air force was allowed to carry out surveillance from the air-space and to monitor the implementation of the agreement on the ground. The Operation Joint Guarantor involved the deployment of NATO forces to Macedonia, the official interpretation was that the forces were there to provide support to the verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija, and if necessary they could be deployed to protect them and to cover their withdrawal from the area. That mission, that operation launched by NATO forces was launched on the basis of a decision of the NATO Council of the 11th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to this information, there were 1.850 soldiers who were to be deployed as part of that operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. According to our information, that was the strength. You can see here it specified the assets that were also to be deployed. There were also the UNPREDEP forces deployed in Macedonia, some other forces, too. And we had a great deal of understanding for the forces deployed there, but naturally we were a bit cautious about that, too, because those forces gradually increased in size as the Operation Joint Guarantor developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was the Army of Yugoslavia informed about this operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, that operation was launched on the -- established on the 11th of November, 1998. At that time I was not in the General Staff and I cannot now remember whether it was officially announced, but as far as I know -- or at least I never saw any such document indicating that NATO had officially informed the Yugoslav authorities that such an operation was being carried out. I think that had that happened, that would have built trust and would have decreased the tensions that were the consequence of it as a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, is there a difference between the Eagle Eye and Joint Guarantor or are these names for the same operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there is a difference. Operation Joint Guarantor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be clear. It's not clear to me at the moment what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, first of all, I see that you have your notebook here, but please put it away because Judges prefer witnesses to answer without taking recourse to their notes, but could you please tell the Trial Chamber very briefly what was the difference between those two operations, Eagle Eye and Joint Guarantor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well as I said, Eagle Eye was an operation that had been agreed between the Yugoslav authorities and NATO immediately after the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was signed on the 13th of October, 1998. In this operation -- as part of this operation a group of NATO officers were to be deployed to the air force command of the VJ and a group of VJ officers was also to be at the NATO air force command at Vicenza. The purpose of this exchange of officers was to build trust and to monitor the situation on the ground, that was the purpose of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you now please tell us about the Operation Joint Guarantor because General Smiljanic had given us enough information about Operation Eagle Eye?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Operation Joint Guarantor was a ground force operation in Macedonia using ground forces, Eagle Eye involved the air force and Joint Guarantor involved the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you told me you that didn't know whether the VJ had been informed about Joint Guarantor. But can I now ask you while you were the chief of intelligence operations at the VJ did the VJ get any information from NATO regarding Operation Joint Guarantor, for instance, any increases in the number of troops or any new assets that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we didn't get such information directly from the competent persons in NATO. There was just some communiques, some press releases meant for the public, and then we of course received it -- those releases, and we checked whether they corresponded to the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, does it follow that Joint Guarantor is not an operation involving the VJ or Yugoslavia, whereas Eagle Eye was such an operation? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's the way I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did -- who was the witness who mentioned this before, Smiljanic, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Smiljanic spoke in detail about Eagle Eye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he give the name Eagle Eye to it because I must have been asleep at that point? It's the sort of name that would stick in the mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he did, but I believe these two witnesses are talking about the same operation from the description given by General Krga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was just surprised I didn't remember the name, that's all. Mr. Krga, we have to break at this stage for 20 minutes for various reasons. While we have the break could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are still with Exhibit P936, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, at the end of every briefing you made, you formulated something you called conclusions. In this specific case as well at the end of the collegium meeting, if I can summarize it, you gave three conclusions; first, that finding a political solution for the crisis was complex because there was no readiness to exert pressure on the KLA; second, that there is no alternative position to the one propounded by the United States; and third, that Albanian official authorities are providing ever more important support to the KLA. Now, what were these conclusions to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: After presenting the information and data that I was able to collect and analyse together with my colleagues and that I considered important for the collegium, I informed them, therefore, and then offered some conclusions regarding changes in trends in the security situation around our country. And when I thought it necessary, I also offered proposals as to what should be done to relieve tensions or to improve the situation or resolve specific problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I see in this text that you propose the existing measures of combat-readiness to stay in place and not to change?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that was a proposal or a suggestion to the Chief of the General Staff, one I determined that security indicators in the region had not changed significantly, that there was no threat to the security of our country, so that the measures taken on a regular basis in our army were sufficient and there was no need for anything to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 3D559.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are now going to move to the collegium meeting that took place two weeks later on the 28th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we have page 5 in B/C/S and 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At this meeting you informed the members of the collegium about the accelerated build-up of air and naval forces of NATO in the region, mentioning specifically aircraft carriers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. We monitored activities in the region, and whenever a change occurred, we would register it and analyse possible reasons for it. Fortunately, in the greatest number of cases the changes that took place were regular and planned by NATO and did not reflect directly on the security and defence of our country. However, in certain crisis situations when the situation was not good and when it kept deteriorating, we had to evaluate whether those changes in the level of forces in the region, air forces, naval forces, and ground forces resulted as a reaction to the developments in Kosovo and Metohija primarily. We tried to exert maximum -- to act responsibly and to objectively evaluate whether those were regular activities or a reaction to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we lower page 6 till the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference on this page to the accelerated build-up of air and naval forces of NATO?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second half of the page, that's why I wanted it scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S is okay. The English needs to be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't remark that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, among other things, you noted here that the number of aircraft was raised by 128 from 264 to 392, the number of warships by 16, et cetera, but I want to ask you about the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page for the Trial Chamber, page 7, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] I'm sorry, page 6, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What you concluded, General, is this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel indicate what he's reading, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, can you identify the part that you're reading in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's first sentence towards the top of page 7. The beginning is on page 6 and I'm reading it all, it continues on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So the whole sentence is: "Exercising the activities of mixed assault forces on targets on the ground and applying the AWACS engagement zone, indicate a possibility of testing plans and operational exercises and procedures in the case of possible intervention against the FRY." General, could you comment in keeping with what you just said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Right. In addition to monitoring quantitative changes, that is changes in the numbers of certain assets of armed forces, such as planes, ships, tanks, et cetera, we also monitored qualitative changes in terms of behaviour and activities. This conclusion results from our analysis of their regular training and activities they performed, but we must also recall that plans for possible intervention against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been made back in the summer of 1998. And proceeding from that, therefore, we analysed whether those activities were in any way related to possible preparations for an intervention of those forces against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 6, the third paragraph in English, thank you, and page 6 in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this information that you had in relation to the forces in Italy reads: "It is typical that Italy keeps making announcements about the possibility of deploying NATO forces, reinforcing NATO forces in Albania, which is primarily intended to prevent a possible exodus of Albanian refugees to the west." My question is: At that time, General, there were no refugees in the territory of Kosovo that was end January 1999, so what is this information related to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As you well know, Italy had even previously had problems coming from the territory of Albania by sea and in other ways, and you remember the crisis in 1996 and early 1997. So probably by that time there were already several dozen refugees from Kosovo and Metohija who turned up in Italy wanting possibly to move on to third countries in Europe, western Europe. Italy wanted to prevent this by creating certain conditions in northern Albania or Albania in general to admit those refugees, and once the necessary prerequisites are in place to return them to Kosovo and Metohija. I cannot claim with any certainty that the representatives of Italy already then believed that what later happened in Kosovo would happen and that it would cause a large number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in the conclusion on this page you mention a term "operationalisation of the strategy." Can you -- of military threat,"the operationalisation of the strategy of military threat." Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, it was evaluated that several moves had been made by foreign factors, diplomatic, media, and other contacts with our representatives indicated without any doubt that the use of military force served to support diplomatic and all the other activities that were under way, and this pressure needed to be convincing. To make it convincing, the army was often used to make displays of force and other activities to show that the diplomatic initiatives were serious and needed to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Army of Yugoslavia in its turn monitored these activities and prepared it own evaluations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have 3D685. It's an evaluation of the security situation and security threats to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that's the title of the document. We will have it on the screen soon, 3D685.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what is the difference between the evaluation you presented regularly at collegium meetings and this type of evaluation provided in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, we monitored the situation daily and evaluated it daily, and if there were any significant changes in news, we would immediately inform the General Staff and others. We did it regularly at collegium meetings that were held, as a rule, once a week. However, when a number of serious events that required a more comprehensive and deeper evaluation and that affected our defence and security had accumulated, we prepared such evaluations once in several months or once a month once we had more comprehensive idea of what was going on around our borders and in our region. And we tried to derive conclusions about what needed to be done in our army to be able to respond adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, your administration prepared which parts of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, from the very nature of our work, you can see which segments we prepared, primarily the influence of the internal factor and further developments envisaged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Influence of the foreign factor and further developments envisaged, again in the light of the influence of the foreign factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 6, please. The second half, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, you explain at greater length the influence of the United States on NATO and you use again that term "using a military political organization as an instrument to control the crisis." This document was done sometime in February 1999. Do you know the intent behind it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: The intent behind this document was the same as for the previous ones, that is, to provide as realistic an evaluation as possible of the development of the situation and the tendencies and to see at the level of the General Staff what needed to be done to provide the most adequate response.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page -- sorry, page 9 in B/C/S, it's paragraph 2, and page 9 in English, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I just asked you about the information concerning the preparations of the Italian government for the establishment of humanitarian refugee camps in northern Albania, and you gave us your response. However, in this text some precise numbers are mentioned, 200 to 500.000 refugees are mentioned as possibly arriving. Who provided this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We received this information from our sources in Italy. The source said that they thought that this number of refugees was possible and that preventive action had to be taken by Italy, NATO, and other western countries in order to respond to this situation. To the best of my recollection, we did not get any precise confirmation as to the basis on which the Italian government assessed this -- that this number of refugees could possibly arrive. I'm not saying that they foresaw the conflict or the air-strikes or anything else that might lead to such consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please look at page 10 in English, paragraph 3, that's page 9 in B/C/S, the last paragraph. There is a conclusion here which says: "These activities can be connected to the plans for possible KLA spring offensive which would probably start with incidents along the border with Albania. It is planned that they should be provoked by terrorists from Kosovo and Metohija, and by the Albanian Army personnel with the aim of dragging the Yugoslav Army into direct conflict which they expect would be cause for a NATO intervention."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we had several pieces of information indicating that among the Albanian extremists there was a tendency to cause conflicts which might lead to a NATO military intervention, probably because they thought that a NATO military intervention or a conflict between Yugoslavia and NATO would enable them to achieve the goals they were fighting for. And we have just seen this in recent days and their aim was an independent state of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 19 in B/C/S and 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, does that mean that your view at that time was that if the KLA got involved in an offensive in the spring, that would be enough to draw NATO into the matter? Was that seriously the Yugoslav position at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could not know at the time exactly whether that would be sufficient for NATO to get involved, but we did have information indicating that were a widespread conflict to break out, NATO might get involved. We were certainly the last ones who wanted such a conflict because we knew what it could lead to. We had a realistic assessment of the forces of our country and of NATO, and of course we wished to avoid such a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand all of that. It's the concept that NATO would enter a conflict to support an apparently terrorist organization and that that alone might be sufficient to bring them in, and that was seriously your view at that time? You may be right. I just want to be clear that it was as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
