utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We didn't think NATO could be so naive or that the NATO countries would simply respond to certain initiatives coming from an organization such as the KLA, that's quite clear. But we did think that the KLA activities we had information were being prepared could realistically lead to an escalation of the conflict. Because if KLA units and KLA elements attacked the army or the police, the army and the police could not, of course, remain passive, they would have to defend themselves, they would have to respond. And this then would lead to an escalation of the violence, and we know what the characteristics of that violence were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, it says quite simply that you envisaged a KLA spring offensive which would probably start with disputes along the border with the aim of drawing the army into the conflict, which they suspect -- which they suspect would be cause for a NATO intervention. And "they," I assume, is the KLA, but what I was trying to find out was whether you seriously thought that that would be enough to bring NATO in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't think it would be enough to draw NATO into the conflict, but we did have information from sources close to the Albanian factors and we conveyed their expectations. They were the ones who felt that by causing conflicts they could provoke a NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, the witness has already spoken about this, but I wish to draw your attention to the fact that on page 10 of the English, paragraph 4, and on page 11, last paragraph, and page 12, paragraph 1, there are more details about the NATO plans which include an operation -- the guarantor operation, Joint Guarantor Operation. Could we now go to page 20 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you prepared a scenario envisaging the course of events, it says here that "unless an agreement is reached," what agreement is being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As we know, there were negotiations under way in Rambouillet at the time and a little later in Paris. We followed the course of these negotiations closely because we knew that if they were successful further escalation of the conflict would be avoided; if they failed, however, then very unfavourable developments would ensue, and unfortunately this proved to be correct. One of the methods of work in our General Staff, just as in any other General Staff in the world, is to predict possible developments and various possibilities. We planned for two eventualities: If an agreement was reached and if an agreement was not reached. Based on the information we had, we analysed the possible consequences. At the time this was one view of the possible further development of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This scenario includes 12 points?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, there are 12 points here, and were we now to analyse them we could easily see what points were actually shown to be correct and which ones did not happen. Unfortunately, most of what we foresaw actually did happen, and I say "unfortunately," because an unfavourable course of events ensued, leading to war and all the other things we know happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, not to go into details now. Can you answer the following: In relation to point 3, "further destabilisation of the FRY," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was this confirmed by later developments?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, partly. One of the goals was to change the then-leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's enough, General. I only wanted you to tell me whether it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Point 6, again --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And point 12, the Contact Group and the ultimatum to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Point 11: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no new resolution until the end of the armed conflict, that was Resolution 1244.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you have now before you the whole list of 12 points. Are there any other points which were not fully confirmed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, most of the others, yes, for the most part all the others were confirmed by later events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 23 and 24 in B/C/S and page 25 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have conclusions before us, again, General, and I'm primarily interested in conclusion number 5. The entire team of the General Staff worked on these conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the methods of work. When such serious documents were being compiled, not only did every administration or sector do the work falling within its field of work, but there were also meetings where opinions and conclusions were exchanged and these follow from one such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Point 5 of this document, the primary aim of our country would be to avoid an armed conflict with NATO. Is that the principle that the Army of Yugoslavia adhered to throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As I already said, we analysed the situation and we knew very well what military resources NATO had at its disposal, and of course we were not so naive as to wish to enter into that conflict, on the contrary, we wished to avoid it. We demonstrated that in our numerous contacts with foreign military and other representatives, but unfortunately our activity and our efforts were unsuccessful and the conflict did break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P941, please, that's a collegium meeting of the 25th of February, 1999, page 4 in B/C/S and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this collegium meeting took place after the negotiations in Rambouillet, I believe. Could you please comment on what you see before you. It's in the middle of the page. You provided four points as to what the FRY should do after these negotiations. The first one is to -- it concerns the already -- the positions already gained; and secondly, to show a high level of readiness to defend itself without being provoked and blamed for armed conflicts; third, a high degree of cooperation; and fourth, to prepare documents against the bringing of foreign troops to Kosovo and Metohija. Well, my question concerns the bringing in of foreign troops in Kosovo and Metohija, and that was one of the demands being put by the international community very strongly at the time. What was the context of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As we know, this was mentioned at the negotiations in Rambouillet and our representatives who were there would probably be able to speak about this better, but evidently there was an interest in bringing NATO forces into Kosovo and Metohija. We analysed the reasons for this interest, and there were two main points being put. One, that probably in some circles among the international institutions, they thought that without these international forces in Kosovo and Metohija the conflict could not be resolved peacefully or it would be very difficult to resolve it peacefully; and secondly, we thought at the time that it was possible that some other strategic interests were involved which they wanted to implement by bringing these forces into Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says here: "Various pieces of information indicate that despite their claims these foreign troops would not completely disarm the so-called KLA, the Albanians are even bragging that Mrs. Albright has promised them that NATO troops will make sure they will hold a referendum even if there was no such provision in the agreement."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information we had. The Albanians bragged about this. They said they had been given a promise that it was crucial for international forces to enter Kosovo and Metohija, and they would then make possible what they aspired to, which is either a referendum or some other method of gaining independence. Because of this, of course, we were concerned. We were concerned that bringing in those forces would infringe on our territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On the following page, page 5 in both versions, you had a specific proposal to make to the Chief of General Staff, that is, that representatives of the General Staff should become involved in further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. As we analysed the characteristics of the Rambouillet talks and the talks in Paris, and bearing in mind the experience from Dayton and looking at how some other countries were dealing with that, primarily the United States of America, where politicians and diplomats are regularly accompanied by members of the military, generals, or rather, officers, we felt that it would be good for our delegation to include army personnel for two basic reasons. The first reason was that they were in a position to give suggestions to our diplomats on a number of issues that pertained to the military, the use of the military, cooperation with the other armies, and so on; and the second reason was that it was quite apparent that among the elements that were being negotiated were issues that related directly to the army, the withdrawal of the troops, bringing in of other forces into this area, cooperation with those forces, and other issues that in our view could be dealt with by the army personnel in a much more professional manner than by those people who did not have the necessary expertise, civilian diplomats and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I guess you had an opportunity to talk about all that with General Ojdanic. What was his position on all that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: He supported this idea, and as far as I can remember he presented it to the state authorities. Now, as to what happened later, I don't know, but in essence the result is quite clear. None of the representatives of the army attended those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next exhibit is P935, please, page 6, paragraph 3 in B/C/S; page 7, paragraph 1 in the English version. Again, this is the collegium meeting of the 11th of March, 1999, so a couple of weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in this paragraph you mentioned some new elements that pertained to the forces in the region. Let me just say, first of all, that a new Joint Command was established in Skopje under the command of General Michael Jackson, and the rapid reaction force has a total of 9.500 troops. Here you give an assessment as to what those forces were capable of, and could you please comment on it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I've already indicated, we monitored very closely all the developments in our region, and in those weeks the events in Macedonia were at the forefront. We noticed that there was an increase in those forces, not only in terms of their personnel strength, but also the structure changed. Elements that were brought in were the elements that could lead one to the conclusion that those forces could be assigned different tasks, not just to help pull out the members of the verification mission. This primarily could be seen from the presence of tanks, armoured personnel carriers, artillery weapons that were also deployed in those units. Analysing the developments at that time, the situation was quite tense, there were some indications, some announcements that the verification mission would withdraw, we felt that those forces were there to support the withdrawal of the verifiers, but that it was also possible that they could be used for some other purpose. We felt that there were two options. The first one was that once an agreement was reached to find a political solution for the crisis, that they could be deployed in Kosovo and Metohija as a peace force of some kind; and the second option was the assumption on our part that it was possible that they were getting ready to enter into Kosovo and Metohija by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Let us move on to the next exhibit, that's P938, page 5, paragraph 1 in Serbian; and page 5, it's the second -- the bottom half of the page in B/C/S. So this is the collegium of the 18th of March. General, you can see right there at the top you say, as regards the military measures, the pressure, that will continue. And in the key moments of the talks, one step further could be taken with threats of force in such a way that all the indicators of aggression against the FRY could be found. And you forecast that the verifiers could withdraw to Macedonia, the power to authorise air-strikes would be transferred from Solana to Clark and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we're now on 18th of March, there was this danger that the Paris talks could fall through. As we saw, the forces in our region grew in size. Incidents on the ground in Kosovo and Metohija also grew more frequent, and we made an assessment as to how the situation could develop further. As you noted, we anticipated that the verifiers could withdraw. It was not difficult to make such a forecast, because their plans envisaged such a measure in case of a crisis. But for us, it was a very important indicator because we knew that the verifiers on the ground and those who supported them thought that the situation was so bad that their further presence there was in question. At that time some diplomats already started leaving Belgrade. Forces in the region exhibited signs of upgraded readiness, but there were also indicators that spoke to the opposite, that told us that there was a possibility that NATO forces would not be used against Yugoslavia. By that I mean primarily that at that time in the Adriatic or in the Mediterranean, there were no plane carriers. The Enterprise had been there before, but it left the area. So there were no aircraft carriers in that area. That was quite strange in light of what happened a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in this passage, that's the fourth paragraph in B/C/S, you say this could happen if the Serbian delegation would be blamed as the sole culprit for the failed negotiations and if new conflicts could be provoked in Kosovo involving a larger number of victims, greater destruction, and refugees possibly with the attacks against verifiers, border incidents, and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the forecasts that we made that in our view could lead to a NATO intervention, could be used as a pretext for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could we please -- I'm sorry, I have to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we scroll the English text down as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had experience from the reactions to the Racak incident and the fact that our forces were blamed for that, and of course we feared that something like that could occur again, that there could be another incident that could be used to -- as a pretext for the use of NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on the next page there's another conclusion, that's the next page in English, too, in B/C/S too. You again present a number of conclusions, the Judges will be able to read that in detail, but one of the conclusions that I'm particularly interested in, that I find intriguing, you proposed that letters be sent to some chiefs of General Staffs and that the federal minister be told to do that, too, that the suggestion be made to him, presenting the situation the activities of the Army of Yugoslavia and some proposals would be made in those letters. My question related to this is: Can you tell us something more about the correspondence and indeed the communication between General Ojdanic and General Clark, who was the supreme commander of the NATO forces in that period, or rather, throughout March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As far as I know, in March General Clark and General Ojdanic talked on the phone four times, on the 2nd of February [as interpreted], on the 12th of February [as interpreted], on the 22nd of March, and on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we verify these dates before you go further. Could you give us the dates again, Mr. Krga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 2nd of March, 15th of March, 22nd of March, and 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was present when General Ojdanic spoke to General Clark on some of those occasions. General Ojdanic was quite amenable to General Clark's suggestions, and in the first conversation they tried to exchange their views on the situation in a very calm manner. On that occasion, as far as I can remember, General Clark suggested to General Ojdanic to come to Brussels, where they would then discuss the situation. In the next conversation, General Clark at first offered cooperation, noted that there was a need to avoid conflict, and later on he started issuing threats. He said that if there were a conflict, that the Yugoslav Army would be destroyed, that command structures would be changed, and so on. And I remember the last conversation immediately before the air-strikes began, where General Clark for all intents and purposes issued an ultimatum to General Ojdanic, warning him not to attack NATO forces in the region, in the territory of neighbouring countries. And as far as I can recall, he warned him that our navy ships should not go into open sea. It was a clear indicator as far as we were concerned that the air-strikes were imminent and they, indeed, happened that very evening. Apart from those contacts with General Clark, all of us, depending on our actual job, had a number of diplomatic contacts with a number of representatives from mainly NATO member states, where we wanted to clear the situation up, to get some objective information as to what is happening in Kosovo and Metohija and who was responsible for it. And I remember my meeting with the US military attache, Colonel Pemberton, that was on the 12th of March. We analysed all that, and I proposed to him that there should be an exchange of officers, that NATO representatives should come to Belgrade and that representatives from our country should go to the NATO headquarters, and that some misunderstandings should be resolved quickly in an operational manner. He showed great understanding for this initiative. He went to report to his superiors, and a little while later he told me that the initiative was deemed to be good but that it came too late. So this idea of mine was never implemented. Of course we had contacts with various other representatives, with General Mandelson who -- General Anderson, who was accompanying Mr. Holbrooke and a number of other representatives from various armed forces where we wanted to present our views in quite frank terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Some control over this by you. Do you want all this information; if so, it would be much better if it was coming in response to pointed questions than a several-page account of events in general. I thought you were asking about specific matters, and I want to ask a question myself, if I may, at this stage. But perhaps you want to get this episode dealt with first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this episode is of interest to me. I merely wanted to ask General Krga the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know when this meeting with General Anderson took place, so between General Anderson and General Ojdanic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I think it was on the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I ask the question I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We seem to get confusing evidence about when the bombing actually began. When did it begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, this is a widely known fact. The air-strikes began at around 2000 hours on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the meeting -- sorry, the last discussion on the telephone or radio or whatever between Mr. Ojdanic and -- General Ojdanic and General Clark was earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember at what time, but it was sometime in the morning or around noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there were no air-strikes on the night of the 23rd into the morning of the 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to cut a long story short, I suggest that these exhibits, 3D754, 706, 707, and 3D985 be admitted. They are communications and telephone conversations that General Clark had with General Ojdanic. Some of them have been exhibited already. I believe the witness testified enough about all of them. I suggest they be introduced in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any problem with that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please show the witness 3D894.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you said the air-strikes began on the 24th March. We now see a document dated 26th March called "briefing." Can you tell us what is this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: What is called "briefing" here is not really an official document. It's more of a draft made for myself, as a reminder for reporting at the Chief of the General Staff. It was an evening activity called briefing. We had daily briefings during the war, first around 8.30 p.m. And later at 6.00 p.m. In addition that, every morning we submitted a short brief on the events of the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can I now draw your attention to the penultimate paragraph on the first page in both versions. My question is this: At that time, the Army of Yugoslavia was predicting at that time that there would be a ground intervention in Kosovo as well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Our information at the time indicated that the NATO intervention was planned in three stages. The first: Attacks on air defence and air force systems and the accompanying infrastructure; second -- mainly in Kosovo and Metohija; the second one were attacks on army forces and assets throughout the territory of Yugoslavia; and the third stage would be a ground invasion. That's the information we had then. However, as we all know now, this forecast was not confirmed, there was no classical ground intervention by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 3D898, that's the briefing from 28th March, 1999, and can we please look at paragraph 4 on page 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, an evaluation is mentioned here related to NATO experts. It says that: "Recommendations would be made for a forceful entry into Kosovo and Metohija in the event it is evaluated that our forces were built up to 50.000, and if the number of refugees reaches 500.000." Can you comment, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: That is the information we received from diplomats, that NATO is making evaluations and analysing, so if our forces grow to 50.000 and the number of refugees grows to 500.000, that would be a reason for a ground invasion of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, two paragraphs below you mention: "Key factors in boosting our position and diplomatic initiative remains in the first place."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Throughout the war and even before the war, and after, almost every day of the aggression we kept thinking how to put an end to the attacks and to resume attempts to reach a political situation. We did not only sit and think, we initiated as many actions as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph there is a reference to aircraft EC-130, what kind of aircraft are these?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: They are equipped with a variety of media components and they are used for propaganda, political purposes, that is, from these aircraft you can broadcast, throw leaflets, and try to influence in that way the population on the territory you are flying over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 3D902, it's again a briefing of the 30th of March, 1999, last paragraph in B/C/S, please, thank you, and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You presented another piece of information at this evening briefing, saying that: "In parallel with air-strikes and preparations for the ground intervention, an increasing number of countries is offering mediation." I wanted to ask you, during the war itself can you tell us who made diplomatic initiatives and how and what did the army try to do in this respect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Most of our attention was preoccupied with defence measures and our capacities for diplomatic activity were considerably reduced; however, to the extent possible, we maintained contact through our military attaches and through the military attaches of the countries that still had them in Belgrade so that already after two days of air-strikes, the military attache of Italy asked for a meeting with me to convey the opinion of his leadership, his authorities, as to what should be done to stop the air-strikes. I could see that he was himself rather upset and hard-hit by what was going on on the territory of Yugoslavia and in Belgrade, and I believe he was trying to be helpful by presenting these initiatives. We also had a contact with London, and we wanted to make an initiative towards western countries that we believed could help stop the war and resume political dialogue and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D906, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this briefing you notified that the list of targets was expanded, that's dated 1st April 1999. In what context was this list expanded?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, initially we had information that the intervention could be in three stages, as I explained, ending with a ground invasion. However, it seems that the initial plans were given up early on and the list of targets was revised and expanded every day to include facilities of infrastructure and other targets that were not directly related to the proclaimed objectives of this NATO action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 3D911, please, that's the briefing of 3rd April 1999, last paragraph in page 1, B/C/S, and last paragraph in English, also page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, you are already presenting possible models for resolving the crisis in Kosovo-Metohija, and again you mentioned the context of refugees and their protection. We have two numbers, 630.000 refugees and 500.000, again the same number that could trigger a NATO intervention. The Army of Yugoslavia never treated, or rather, how did the Army of Yugoslavia treat the problem of refugees, the return of refugees, that is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: I must say I was not directly engaged in those affairs, but in the course of briefings and monitoring the responses of important international factors concerning this problem, I tried to help prepare some points for refugees who were either trying to cross the border towards Albania or Macedonia or to return to Kosovo. I thought that this whole thing could lead the western media and western political factors to understand that it was not our objective at all to expel Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the second part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is a current meeting of intelligence services chiefs and various forms of support and assistance to the KLA including weapons in order for the KLA to be used as some sort of advanced force by NATO. What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We had a body of information at the time about the cooperation of KLA with various NATO elements, and we had information, among others, that this meeting mentioned here reviewed this issue as well. Highly placed officials of a number of countries made announcements that air-strikes would continue until a balance is struck between the strength of the Army of Yugoslavia and the KLA. Under those circumstances, then political negotiations would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also present certain conclusions and proposals at the end of this briefing. Again you mention diplomatic initiative, you have already discussed this. What about the second proposal related to posts or points for refugees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, the idea was to really help those people, and also to show the world that the Army of Yugoslavia and our police forces were not trying in any way to expel the refugees from Kosovo, it was not in their interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 3D913. It's a briefing of the 4th of April, first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, there's a conclusion here: "The choice of targets does not seem to follow a political or military logic," that's paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: On the eve of the war and during the war, we had the opportunity to observe the doctrine of NATO in action, and what we knew about it did not correspond to what we could see on the ground. In Vojvodina, in -- on the Hungarian border there were also attacks, there were attacks on bridges and similar facilities, and all of this did not seem to correspond to the principles and the doctrine of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at paragraph 2. It says: "There are speculations about the deployment of a large NATO force to Albania which would be engaged in a peacekeeping mission," et cetera. And the passage that says: "This should be seen as linked to the existence of plans for a step-by-step operation." What kind of plan was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We had information that the KLA was planning to engage its own armed forces, but also refugees, to capture the territory, the border belt with Albania and Macedonia step by step, putting back our forces and disabling them from further action or police action, creating a corridor for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, this last piece of information from the sources that informed you, it says: "Some sources indicate that the Siptars have been set in motion as part of this plan in order to separate them from the VJ units which have thus become open targets for the aggressor." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. During those NATO actions, Albanian civilians were sometimes casualties, probably because of the lack of precision or the fact that those people could not be separated from the military targets that were close to them, and the information that we got was that the purpose behind all this was to separate the Albanians from our forces, thus isolating our forces and leaving them with no possibility of taking any precautions and they could then be targeted more successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D918.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is the briefing of the 7th of April. Could you please look at paragraph 4 in -- under item 2, which begins with the words: "A total of 335 air sorties took place during the past 24 hours ..." There's something handwritten here. Could you please read this sentence that says: "As we announced, this was the most massive deployment of the air force by the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that by hand in response to our press release on the cessation of operations, because our government unilaterally on the 6th of April, I think, that was on Easter, issued a communique calling for the cessation of further combat operations, at least during the Easter holidays. This did not happen. This might be a coincidence. I cannot now claim that this was in direct response to this communique on the part of the federal government, but that was our opinion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Attached to this document you provide your view of the ground operation, or rather, preparations for such an operation, that's page 3 in the B/C/S version and I think it's also page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it's page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a document that contains a lot of detail. What I'm interested in is the follow, General, these are the forces that NATO had at its disposal, they're listed under A and B. So this -- these are the forces that NATO had deployed in Albania and Macedonia at the time or is this the projected increase in their strength?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: No, no. This -- these are the forces that we established were present in Macedonia and Albania at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So I don't want to read all that. It speaks for itself. We have A and B in the English version, that's what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, could we break at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, we have to have another break for half an hour at this stage. Would you please again leave with the courtroom with the usher. We'll see you at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova has been struggling through either a heavy cold or influenza over the past few days and we have decided it's in her best interest to go home and rest up and try to keep with us. So in the interests of justice, we continue in her absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have Exhibit P929 brought up on e-court, please, page 3 in Serbian and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a collegium of the 9th of April, 1999. You compiled a separate special assessment for that collegium meeting. Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This was one of those situations where after almost two weeks of war we wanted to have a more detailed overview of the development of the situation and the possible further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. So that was one of those assessments you said contained information covering a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, one of those compiled from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 1, and then it says the proclaimed aims of the aggression in the middle of the paragraph: "Were first to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe, second to neutralise the military power of the FRY and third, preserve the credibility of the US and NATO, while the actual aim of the aggression was to punish the FRY and force it to accept the peace agreement which would provide for the arrival of NATO forces in Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say the seizure of territory from the FRY." This initial standpoint of yours, could you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we did have such information. In the beginning when the possibility of air-strikes was mentioned, the credibility of NATO was emphasised as a reason. It's possible that the credibility of NATO was linked to events on the ground and most of all with what they referred to as the humanitarian catastrophe. These goals changed in the course of combat activities and were later expressed in the form of those five demands of NATO which are widely known.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at page 8 of this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll go back to these conclusions of yours. It's the paragraph before the last of your intervention where you say that: "The commitment to the peace option of the FRY could best attach value to the efforts hitherto and there would be a danger of devaluing what had been achieved so far." Could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of our strongest standpoints, to try to resolve the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija through the peace option because, as I said, a further continuation of war would bring with it many risks; unfortunately, this proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to go through the entire document with the witness. It was my intention, rather, to draw attention to what the witness said in full. In English it's on pages 4 to 8 and in B/C/S from page 3 to page 8, and now I'd like to move on to the next exhibit, 3D934, page 2 in B/C/S and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a briefing of the 21st of April, 1999. I won't go into detail because the Chamber can find all the details it needs in the document. What I'm interested in is the part you entitled "proposals." In the second half of April, in your view, some peace initiatives you thought could be brought to life. What did you think, could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, this was a time when the summit in Washington was being prepared on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of NATO. We monitored the reactions of the members of NATO and we saw among them there were those who would be interested in having the war come to an end as soon as possible. I wanted to draw attention to this issue and to say that these factors should be supported through possible contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn the page in English, page 3. Yes, that's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And at the end of these proposals which contain three points, you provide some information linked to the information that the intelligence administration obtained and it has to do with conversations among NATO pilots.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. On television the pilots' conversations were broadcast after they had bombed a column of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. After that we obtained information that in NATO they had concluded that we were monitoring some of their conversations, and then according to our information they started using a completely closed communication system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And from that point on you could no longer monitor NATO pilots' conversations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: No, we could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 3D938, a briefing of the 25th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in paragraph 6 of this document. It mentions the so-called plan 4. Can you please tell us what sort of plan this was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We knew that a number of plans were being drawn up in NATO concerning the intervention in Yugoslavia, some of them had already been implemented and some of course were fortunately never implemented. Clark said in an interview that there were 12 to 15 such plans. We had information that plan 4 was, in fact, a plan for a ground force operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And paragraph 7 of this document, the Kuks Garrison in Albania is fully controlled by US officers. Can you tell us where the Kuks Garrison is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It's very close to the border with Kosovo and Metohija, with Serbia on the River Drin, and it's practically only a few kilometres away from the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 3D940, it's the briefing of the 27th of April, page 1, last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on page 1, paragraph 3, it says that everything indicates that NATO force activity was not to be expected, but rather NATO -- Albanian activity and that they were being trained and equipped mostly in Albania for the purpose of their infiltration in Kosovo and Metohija. This is in April, the 27th of April, 1999. In your statement you described in detail the offensive waged by the KLA against the forces of the FRY. Can you please comment on this in the context of this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As I said, there was quite a lot of information indicating that a possible ground force operation could be launched, but also another version of a ground force operation which would involve sending KLA forces over the border from Albania. This was carried out between the 9th and the 10th of April until the 26th of May in the area of Kosare which is to the south towards Prizren, and this operation did not yield the expected results as planned by the KLA, so that later on it was transferred to the north. The name of the operation was Arrow, Strela, on the Vrbnik axis where significant forces were deployed in order to break through on to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 72, 10, after the word "could be launched," the witness I believe said "by NATO," "a ground force attack could be launched by NATO," that was one of the versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this information you mention certain misunderstandings about the large-scale engagement of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. There was information about how these forces should be commanded and we also knew that some of the Albanian refugees and those who had been mobilised into those units did not wish to get involved in such actions and that there were some misunderstandings which we monitored as far as we were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D600, this is the briefing of the 30th of April, 1999, and this is -- well, these are the minutes, actually, of the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 1 there's a summary of what you said, and you said: "Increased activity for three reasons: First, the weather is better; secondly, fuel tanks have been secured; and three --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat point 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Analysing the tempo of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Point 3 was: "Chernomyrdin's visit."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Analysing the bombing in the various stages of the war, we registered a phenomenon which was quite telling. There was always more intensive activity just before the launching of a peace initiative. I cannot say that this was calculated to increase the pressure, but there was an evident correspondence between those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D955, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, again, this is a briefing. This time the date is the 12th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please have page 3 in English and page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Again we have the proposals that would prove our readiness to find a political solution for the conflict, the return of the refugees, withdrawal of units, and again we have the second proposal, that the commission for assessing war damage should send a request to the United Nations to see the degree of destruction and magnitude of the suffering of the civilian population. General, I know that we have been revisiting this several times already, but could you please tell us what was the context in which those proposals were made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We used every option at our disposal, every initiative on the part of the international players that was aimed at finding a peaceful solution for the conflict and ending the war. Our proposals were to support those initiatives, to do something concrete. Here I propose that the issue of the return of the refugees should be addressed and possible withdrawal of our units to garrisons away from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. All of this was aimed to create conditions for the cessation of the air-strikes and to launch political dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the return of the refugees was a fact that the military counted on. Were there any contrary views in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, based on all my contacts with all my colleagues in the Supreme Command Staff and further away, I never heard any reaction on anyone's part to the fact that the aim was to expel the refugees. As you can see, we proposed various measures, we even took some measures to create conditions for their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Defence Exhibit 3D968, page 2 in B/C/S and page 2 in English. This is the briefing of the 25th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what I want to know here --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2, both in B/C/S and in English, I'm interested in the comment, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is this information that you presented to the Supreme Command Staff that the refugees were returning and that 4.000 refugees came back through Djeneral Jankovic through Macedonia in a single day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information we had, and as far as you can see and as far as I know, those refugees came back. And the Army of Yugoslavia did not do anything to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 3D969, please. This is the briefing of the 26th of May, 1999. What I'm interested in is page 1 of this document, midway down this page, paragraph 2, the third passage, beginning with the words: "By 1200 hours about 400 sorties have been recorded." I'm now waiting for the English text to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So this is yet another day, the 26th of May, 1999, where we have the increased air-strike activities including the actions by strategic bombers, B-52 and B-1B. First of all, General, could you tell me the strategic bombers, B-52 and B-1B, what kind of aircraft are these? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, as you can judge from their name, these are strategic bombers. They carried a lot of payload, heavy payload. They came from airports located both in the European member NATO states and from the US. They carried cruise missiles in most cases and they didn't enter our air-space. They were able to fire those missiles from as far as Balaton and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say here that the list of targets would be expanded again in order to exert pressure in the face of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that was yet another such occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the passage immediately below this one you're talking about the NATO air force providing support to the KLA for executing a breakthrough on the front line?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we were talking about. There was this transfer of action from Kosare to Vrbnik and it was quite indicative that we saw that in this period we recorded intense NATO air force activity, and we established a connection between that increase and those efforts by those forces to penetrate into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 3D978, which is a briefing of the 4th of June, 1999, an intelligence briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 2 in Serbian and page 2 in English there is mention of: "Responses to our acceptance of the principle -- principles, or rather, the positions of the Italian General Staff," if I'm right. Could you please comment briefly because the text speaks for itself. What is this about and how did you get this information.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, this was one of the responses we registered and we attached great importance to it because it came from a significant institution, the General Staff of a prominent and large NATO country. As you can see, there are quite a few standpoints here which later proved to be correct and we received this information through our sources in Rome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now see P1748.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were a part of the delegation of the Army of Yugoslavia which conducted negotiations with authorised representatives of NATO and the Russian Federation on issues of the implementation of the plan of the European Union and the Russian Federation and the signing of the documents comprising the plan of withdrawal of the units. This was in Kumanovo. Can you tell us very briefly how these negotiations were conducted, with what authority, and what was their result?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: As we can see, negotiations were conducted with the authority given to the delegation by General Ojdanic, and the aim was quite clear, to arrive at a Military Technical Agreement with NATO representatives based on the Ahtisaari-Chernomyrdin document which had been accepted, and thereby to create the conditions for the Security Council resolution. We have to say that at the airport near Kumanovo where the NATO HQ was, General Jackson and his associates received us very correctly. And in three days of negotiation, we managed to arrive at a document which is entitled Military Technical Agreement, and I think it's widely known. I can say that we as a delegation of the Army of Yugoslavia had the ability to comment on everything that was in the text we received. Part of our comments were accepted and part not, and the text that is known to the public was then agreed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krga, was General Clark still the NATO commander at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now I would like to go through some documents with you. You've spoken about the events that are discussed in those documents in various ways, either in your statement or in your evidence here. So first I would like to see 3D753. In your statement in paragraph 4 you mention a proclamation made by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to Albanians, telling them not to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please have the first and the second pages of that document. Could we have the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, is this the document that was issued by the Army of Yugoslavia, a proclamation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you now with any precision whether this is the document, whether it contains all the elements, but I do know that such a proclamation was made, the purpose was quite sincere. In difficult times, an effort was made to influence the situation, to calm it down, and to have those Albanians and all the others who had left their homes come back, and to seek a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to see 3D783, please. This is report number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me, we've just seen what you said in the collegium meetings and we saw this voluminous intelligence assessment that was -- that covered the period of several months. We saw the briefings that you presented -- the reports that you presented at the evening briefings at the Supreme Command Staff during the war. Could you now tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: This is a report that we sent to the subordinate commands. There were two kinds of such reports. One presented the overall situation for a given day, and the second kind of report dealt with a specific issue. They were distributed only to those commands and units that in our view would be interested in the intelligence presented therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document dated the 29th of March you have information that in the villages and towns in Kosovo and Metohija in the ranks of the KLA there are infiltrated members of the intelligence and security services of the USA and some western countries, whose task is to coordinate with the KLA, in brief.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the intelligence that we received, and we relayed this to the 3rd Army command so that they could pay attention and to see whether this really happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 3D782. This is yet another such report sent to the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This one is dated the 3rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, this was yet another such report that was based on the intelligence gathered on the ground. We give the elements that we learned. The purpose is again to warn our colleagues in the 3rd Army to focus their attention and to prevent any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm interested in particular in the last passage here which reads: "With regard to this western intelligence sources are using confidential intelligence sources to plant information among the Siptars in the diaspora that within the next 24 to 48 hours NATO be begin indiscriminate bombing of Kosovo and Metohija; in other words, it is preparing to raze Kosovo to the ground."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: In addition to the information and intelligence that we received and that we judged to be probable and accurate, it is quite natural that given the context of the war there was information that was planted, as we say it, in order to gain some profit for those who planted this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have another such report dated the 5th of April, 1999, and that's 3D781. It's very brief. "In connection with the attempt by NATO to infiltrate large groups of Siptars and special forces supported by air-strikes," and that's the 5th of April, 1999. In your statement you testified that the KLA attacks from the territory of Albania began on the 10th. Does this report have anything to do with the attack which started on the 10th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, this was one of the pieces of information obtained from the ground, and most probably it proved to be correct because, as we know, several days after that the kind of attack described in this text actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D779, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the 13th of April, 1999, and the list of addressees is a bit broader than in the case of the last report, General. Previously we had the -- mostly the 3rd Army as the addressee; however, here we see it was sent to all units at strategic locations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, we thought that based on the content of each report we should decide who it should be sent to, so sometimes it was sent to just one command, sometimes to two or three, and sometimes to all of them. And this depended on the information actually contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, in the report, you already mentioned 9.000 soldiers in northern Albania, 2.500 Americans with 24 Apache helicopters and 18 multiple rocket-launchers, what is the significance of this piece of information, 24 Apache helicopters?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: We got this information from official information coming from the NATO structures that 24 of these helicopters were being transferred from Germany, first to Albania, and then with the idea of using them in Kosovo and Metohija for combat. Apache are very up-to-date helicopters equipped with armour-piercing rockets, and we were afraid that they might be used in Kosovo and Metohija or some other area because we knew in Iraq, for example, using these helicopters a large number of tanks had been placed out of combat or destroyed. We were faced with the threat that these would be used, but they were not actually used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D772, and this is a report of the 4th of May, 1999, page 2, paragraph 1 in English; page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the possibilities considered here of a NATO ground force operation being launched, and please look at the second paragraph in heading 2. "According to intelligence information, NATO is planning a total blockade of the routes." The use of Apaches that you just described is mentioned here. Would you comment on the following: "Apaches would be used once all the routes were cut off, and the refugees removed from the border area."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. Probably in the tactics of the use of Apaches these contain the -- that the goals, that is, the APCs and tanks, should be out in the open and this would make it easier for them to carry out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D769.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please comment on the first paragraph of this report dated the 12th of May, 1999, and it has to do with the territory of Albania and NATO activities in northern Albania.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. This was information that arrived from the ground at a time when the operation was already under way. This multiple attempt for the KLA to breakthrough on to the territory of Kosovo. This simply confirms what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, it says here that the KLA is carrying out 15-day training under the command of NATO officers.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, we had this information because the KLA did not have all its forces at the front line attempting to breakthrough. It also had forces in the rear, in depth, preparing for new actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D758, report from the intelligence administration dated the 19th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this refers to maps delivered by the KLA to the American representatives of NATO.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes, this is another piece of information from the ground, and we managed to get copies of these sketches which indicate that there was cooperation on the ground between the KLA structures and elements of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the maps are enclosed with this document on pages 2, 3, 4, and 5, and 6. I don't know whether you can see them in the English version, but let's take a look at some of them. Page 6, please. Thank you. 3D762, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I inquire, is there an English version of those maps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because I don't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, CLSS refuses to translate maps and handwriting. We can ask them to do this, but it seems to be their practice. The maps are in the B/C/S version and there is no doubt of their existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say to that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I know we have translations of handwritten diaries and meeting minutes, et cetera. I don't know that they refuse to translate handwriting. And as handwriting goes, this seems to be better than some of the things that have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, these should be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This part of the transcript will be sufficient for me to give to the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, 3D762, this is a report dated the 29th of May, 1999, and it concerns the procurement of weapons. My question is: First, could you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: It's quite clear that members of the KLA procured weapons wherever they could lay hands on it. We tried to monitor all those channels. We were partially successful. This is a piece of information arriving from abroad, indicating that they attempted to purchase weapons in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this quantity of weapons and the sums of money used to pay for them, is information that cannot be concealed from the appropriate services in the countries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that now, I don't know, but after the war we even saw certain films where some of them were bragging that they even managed to get weapons to Kosovo and Metohija from America. We can only assume or speculate whether it was with or without the knowledge of services in those countries or whether they were able to do this completely in secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last document is 3D760.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is another report sent by the intelligence administration dated the 31st of May, 1999. Could you comment on it briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KRGA
utterances.text: Yes. We had several such pieces of information that the extreme wing of the KLA was trying to treat cruelly even Albanians, their compatriots, and consequences such as people leaving their homes, being moved out, possibly murders or burnings of houses were to be blamed on our forces, and this is one such attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if this is a convenient moment, but I have about ten minutes left, perhaps for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid there is another case this afternoon. We can't find any space to overrun even a little to help you, Mr. Visnjic, so we do have to adjourn. I note, however, that you still have two witnesses planned for this week. You're going to have to do something to tailor that evidence to fit. The hours you estimate do not fit into the course of this week. I appreciate the efforts you're making with this witness, but a lot of it is material that you could have presented in writing and you've chosen to do it this way. So you'll have to tailor the rest of your case on the basis we arranged it. Mr. Hannis, you indicated that you would have some -- possibly have something to say about the response to the expert report by yesterday or today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have seen the draft earlier this morning and I know that the comments were made, so I anticipate it will be ready to be filed later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is a written response?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem that raises, of course, is the position of the Defence to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I know, but I think they are such that we did need to put them in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're pointing some specific passages or shortcomings that we find in the report that illustrate the point we're trying to make. I don't think I can do it justice orally at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Krga, we have to terminate our proceedings for today at this stage because there's another case in this court this afternoon; that means you have to come back tomorrow to finish your evidence, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's extremely important that you have no communication or discussion with anybody at all about the evidence in this case, and that means any part of the evidence. You can talk with whoever you like about whatever you like other than the evidence in the case. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
